# Honda Civic Violent Shaking When Put into Reverse or Drive Gears

When a vehicle exhibits violent shaking specifically upon engaging the drive or reverse gears while stationary, the diagnosis almost always points to a load-bearing component rather than an electronic control unit failure. The scenario describedâa 2008 Civic EX sedan with a 5-speed automatic that vibrates only when in gear but not in Park or Neutralâeliminates engine misfires as the primary suspect. If the engine were firing unevenly, you would feel the vibration in Park and Neutral as well. Since the shaking is triggered by the torque converter lock-up or the engagement of the transmission input clutch pack, the issue lies in how that torque is transferred to the chassis.

The most probable culprit is a failed transmission mount, specifically the rear engine/transmission mount. This component acts as a hydraulic shock absorber, isolating the heavy mass of the automatic transmission from the vehicle's subframe. When you shift into Drive or Reverse, the torque converter attempts to move the transmission slightly due to hydraulic pressure and output torque. In a healthy system, the mount compresses to absorb this movement. If the rubber has degraded, cracked, or completely separated from the metal bracket, the engine/transmission assembly becomes loosely suspended within the chassis.

You can verify this hypothesis without lifting the vehicle again. With the car in gear (Drive or Reverse) and the parking brake firmly engaged, have an assistant apply a slight amount of throttle. If the entire front end lurches forward or backward violently, or if you feel a distinct clunking noise as the engine rocks back and forth, the mount is mechanically compromised. This explains why the shaking appeared suddenly; rubber degrades over time due to heat cycles and vibration, often failing completely once it hits a specific temperature threshold or after a minor impact that was previously absorbed.

Another potential issue involves the driveshaft center support bearing on rear-wheel-drive variants or issues with the CV joints on front-wheel-drive models, though less likely given the "stationary" nature of the shake. If the car is stationary and shaking only when torque is applied to the output shaft, a worn center support bearing usually manifests as a whine rather than a violent shake. However, if the driveshaft is out of balance or bent, it can cause vibration that feels worse under load.

A less common but possible cause is the transmission itself developing internal issues, such as a failing torque converter or slipping clutches causing excessive heat and expansion. However, given the user's confirmation that no work was done on the transmission recently, a sudden mechanical seizure of the internal components is statistically improbable compared to external mounting failures. The likelihood of a mount simply snapping or separating from its bracket without prior warning signs like oil leaks (in the case of a torn bushing) is low, but not impossible if the metal bracket sheared off entirely.

Before condemning the transmission, inspect the rubber-to-metal bonding on the rear mount. Look for hairline cracks in the rubber cone that may have expanded into a full separation. If the mount is indeed the cause, replacement is a relatively straightforward job requiring a hoist or jack stands to support the engine weight while removing the old unit and installing a new one. Ensure you replace the fluid as well, as old fluid can contaminate a new mount's hydraulic properties if not flushed properly during reassembly.

If the mounts appear intact and the shaking persists, the next diagnostic step is checking the transmission fluid level and condition with the engine running. Low fluid or fluid that is burnt to the point of blackness could indicate internal slippage or overheating that has warped components, leading to the violent engagement described in the video evidence.
